newsitem.title: UK: Compound found to attack immortality of tumours.
newsitem.headline: Compound found to attack immortality of tumours.

text.p: British and U.S. scientists said on Wednesday they had found a way to target the immortality of tumours and hoped it would eventually lead to new cancer drugs which are much less toxic to patients than those currently in use.
Their compound, a derivative of benzene, affects an enzyme known as telomerase, which research indicates helps cancer cells survive.
Most cells automatically self-destruct when they get too old or are damaged, a process known as apoptosis. But cancer cells do not, growing instead into tumours.

Stephen Neidle of the Institute of Cancer Research in Sutton, near London, and colleagues at the University of Texas at Austin homed in on telomeres. These structures on the ends of chromosomes are associated with the natural death of cells.
Writing in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, Neidle said telomeres normally get knocked shorter and shorter each time a cell divides.
But the enzyme telomerase seems to help stop this process. Up to 90 percent of all human tumour cells contain this enzyme, while most normal cells do not have it.
So Neidle's team went after telomerase, using careful calculations to determine what kind of molecule would best interfere with it.
They found one -- a so-called G-quadraplex interactive compound.
"Since telomerase appears to be found almost exclusively in tumour cells, this type of agent may be useful as model antitumour agents," they wrote in their report in the journal.
They found their compound did indeed inhibit telomerase. "Our next step is to work in cell culture, which we are doing now," Neidle said in a telephone interview.
The research could lead the way to tumour-killing agents that do not make the patient sick.
"That's the goal -- to have nontoxic compound and this is certainly not a very toxic compound," Neidle said.
